title-group.article-title: Nivolumab plus ipilimumab and cobimetinib in previously treated microsatellite-stable/DNA mismatch repair-proficient metastatic colorectal cancer: the phase II CheckMate 142 trial

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have shown limited efficacy in patients with microsatellite-stable/DNA mismatch repair-proficient (MSS/pMMR) metastatic colorectal cancer (CRC). Based on data suggesting antitumor synergy between ICIs and MEK inhibitors, the phase II CheckMate 142 trial evaluated the combination of nivolumab, ipilimumab, and cobimetinib in a cohort of patients with previously treated MSS/pMMR metastatic CRC.

sec.title: Patients and methods
sec.p: Patients received nivolumab (3 mg/kg every 2 weeks), ipilimumab (1 mg/kg every 6 weeks), and cobimetinib [60 mg daily in 28-day cycles (21 days on/7 days off)]. The primary endpoint was investigator-assessed objective response rate (ORR) using RECIST v1.1.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: After a median (range) follow-up of 59.5 (53.9-67.5) months, investigator-assessed ORR in 30 treated patients was 3% (n = 1; with a duration of 32.6 months), disease control rate was 30% (n = 9), and median [95% confidence interval (CI)] progression-free survival was 1.5 (1.4-2.6) months. Median (95% CI) overall survival was 8.2 (2.2-13.9) months. Twenty-five patients (83%) had ≥1 treatment-related adverse event (TRAE), 9 (30%) had a grade 3-4 TRAE, and 3 (10%) discontinued treatment due to TRAEs.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: The combination of nivolumab, ipilimumab, and cobimetinib had limited clinical activity in patients with previously treated MSS/pMMR mCRC. Further investigation of this regimen is not warranted.
Key words: nivolumab, ipilimumab, cobimetinib, metastatic colorectal cancer, MSS/pMMR

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the third most commonly diagnosed cancer worldwide and the second leading cause of cancer death.1 Over the past decade, the treatment landscape for advanced, unresectable CRC has become highly complex with treatment options determined by patient fitness (performance status), primary tumor location, and/or the tumor mutational profile.2,3 Currently recommended therapies for advanced disease include chemotherapies, targeted agents, and immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), either alone or in combination regimens.2,3

CheckMate 142 was an open-label, multicohort, non-randomized, phase II trial of various treatment regimens based on nivolumab (a programmed death 1 ICI) in populations of patients with metastatic CRC. Published data from this trial have provided evidence of the clinical activity of nivolumab monotherapy, nivolumab plus ipilimumab (a cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated protein 4 ICI), and nivolumab plus relatlimab (a lymphocyte activation gene-3 ICI) in patients with previously treated microsatellite instability-high/DNA mismatch repair-deficient (MSI-H/dMMR) metastatic CRC, and of nivolumab plus ipilimumab in patients with untreated MSI-H/dMMR metastatic CRC.4, 5, 6, 7, 8 The latter results supported the phase III CheckMate 8HW trial,9 which led to recent health authority approvals of nivolumab plus ipilimumab for first-line treatment of patients with MSI-H/dMMR metastatic CRC. Nevertheless, efficacy outcomes with ICIs (either as monotherapy or in purely ICI combinations) for treatment of microsatellite-stable/DNA mismatch repair-proficient (MSS/pMMR) metastatic CRC have been poor.10, 11, 12 Based on preclinical and clinical data suggesting antitumor synergy between ICIs and MEK pathway inhibitors,13, 14, 15 CheckMate 142 also evaluated the combination of nivolumab, ipilimumab, and cobimetinib (a MEK inhibitor) in a cohort of patients with previously treated MSS/pMMR metastatic CRC.

sec.title: Study design and patients
sec.p: The overall CheckMate 142 (NCT02060188) study design has been reported previously.6, 7, 8 Briefly, eligible patients were adults (≥18 years of age) with histologically confirmed metastatic or recurrent CRC, an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status (ECOG PS) of 0 or 1, and measurable disease per RECIST v1.1. Patients with a serious uncontrolled medical disorder; active brain or leptomeningeal metastases; active, known, or suspected autoimmune disease; and/or an active malignancy within the previous 3 years (excluding select locally curable cancers) were excluded.

For the current MSS/pMMR cohort, patients were considered eligible if they had a MSS/pMMR phenotype and excluded if they had a known MSI-H/dMMR status, per local testing guidelines. Inclusion in the current cohort also required either (i) progression (during or after) or intolerance to the last administration of approved standard therapies, which must have included a fluoropyrimidine and oxaliplatin or irinotecan, as well as ≥1 of the following (if approved in standard national guidelines): bevacizumab, cetuximab, or panitumumab (if KRAS wild-type), and regorafenib; or (ii) active refusal of chemotherapy (including drugs or biologics) for the treatment of metastatic (stage IV) or locally advanced disease.

For this cohort, patients received nivolumab 3 mg/kg once every 2 weeks, ipilimumab 1 mg/kg once every 6 weeks, and cobimetinib 60 mg daily in a 21 days on/7 days off per 28-day cycle schedule. Dose delays were allowed for all study drugs due to treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs); dose modifications were not permitted for nivolumab and ipilimumab, but allowed for cobimetinib for the management of specified toxicities. Treatment beyond progression was allowed if the patient tolerated the study drug and showed benefit from treatment per investigator assessment. Study treatment continued until disease progression (or discontinuation in patients treated beyond progression), unacceptable toxicity, withdrawal of consent, or study end.

sec.title: Endpoints and assessment
sec.p: Endpoints for CheckMate 142 have been described previously.6, 7, 8 Briefly, the primary endpoint was investigator-assessed objective response rate (ORR), defined as the proportion of patients with a best overall response of complete response (CR) or partial response (PR) per RECIST v1.1. Investigator-assessed ORR was further characterized by evaluation of time to response (TTR), duration of response (DOR), disease control rate (DCR; defined as the proportion of patients with a best overall response of CR, PR, or stable disease for ≥12 weeks), and tumor changes over time. Secondary endpoints were ORR, DOR, and DCR by blinded independent central review (BICR), which were further supplemented by BICR-assessed TTR. Exploratory endpoints included investigator- and BICR-assessed progression-free survival (PFS; defined as time from first dose of study treatment to first instance of documented progression or death due to any cause); overall survival (OS; defined as time from first dose of study treatment to death); and safety.

As described previously,4,5 tumor MSI and/or MMR status was evaluated before screening per local guidelines using immunohistochemistry and/or polymerase chain reaction methods; tumor programmed death ligand 1 expression (≥1% or <1%) was determined from archival or fresh pretreatment tissue samples using the Dako 28-8 pharmDx immunohistochemistry assay (Dako, an Agilent Technologies company, Santa Clara, CA); and BRAF/KRAS mutation status was determined per local guidelines. Tumor mutational burden (TMB) was assessed via whole-exome sequencing of tumor tissue and matching blood as germline control on the Illumina NovaSeq platform (Illumina, San Diego, CA).16

Efficacy and safety assessments have also been described in detail previously.6, 7, 8 In brief, tumor assessments (by computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging) were conducted ≤28 days before first dose, every 6 weeks (±1 week) for 24 weeks, and then every 12 weeks (±1 week) until progression or discontinuation. Objective responses (CR and PR) were confirmed via a second scan carried out ≥4 weeks later. Adverse events (AEs) were assessed continuously using the National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events v. 4.0.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: For the current cohort, sample size calculations were not based on power considerations but were conducted to provide precision on estimation of the ORR. With a projected sample size of 30 patients, an ORR between 13.3% and 36.7% was anticipated to provide meaningful results versus available data for atezolizumab combined with cobimetinib.15 For ORR and DCR, a response rate estimate and associated 95% exact confidence intervals (CIs; calculated by the Clopper–Pearson method) were calculated. All efficacy and safety endpoints were evaluated in patients treated with ≥1 dose of study treatment, except for tumor changes over time, which were assessed in response-assessable patients, defined as those with a target lesion at baseline and ≥1 post-baseline tumor assessment. The Kaplan–Meier method was used for estimates of median DOR, PFS, and OS. Statistical analyses were done using SAS v. 9.2 (SAS Institute, Cary, NC).

sec.title: Patients
sec.p: Between 30 January 2017 and 19 March 2018, 30 patients with previously treated MSS/pMMR metastatic CRC began treatment with nivolumab plus ipilimumab and cobimetinib in CheckMate 142. At clinical cut-off (15 September 2022), median (range) duration of follow-up was 59.5 (53.9-67.5) months. Median (range) age was 54 (39-73) years, 18 patients (60%) were male, and 23 (77%) were white (Table 1). Per investigator assessment, 24 patients (80%) had liver metastases. Fourteen patients (47%) had a KRAS mutation, one (3%) had a BRAF mutation, and 11 (37%) were wild-type for both KRAS and BRAF; the remaining four patients (13%) had unknown mutational status. Almost all patients (n = 29; 97%) had received prior systemic therapy in the metastatic setting (Table 1). At the end of the treatment period, all patients had discontinued study treatment, most commonly because of disease progression (n = 23; 77%); three patients (10%) each discontinued because of study drug toxicity or AEs unrelated to study drug, and one (3%) requested discontinuation of treatment.

sec.title: Efficacy
sec.p: Per investigator assessment, one patient (3%) achieved a confirmed objective response (a PR); their TTR was 3.0 months, and DOR was 32.6 months (Table 2). This patient had confirmed MSS/pMMR status via immunohistochemistry, and had an ECOG PS of 1; stage IV disease at initial diagnosis; a primary rectum tumor; lung and liver metastases; a TMB of 8.29 mutations/Mb; wild-type KRAS and BRAF; and >4 prior systemic therapy regimens. There was high (97%) concordance between investigator-assessed and BICR-assessed ORR, with two patients (7%) achieving a confirmed objective response (both PRs) per BICR (Table 2). Disease control was achieved in nine patients (30%) per both investigator assessment and BICR. In post hoc exploratory analyses, investigator-assessed DCR was numerically higher among patients without versus with liver metastases, patients with an ECOG PS of 0 versus ≥1, and patients with wild-type KRAS/BRAF versus mutated KRAS or mutated BRAF (Supplementary Table S1, available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esmogo.2026.100334). Investigator-assessed tumor changes over time are shown for 22 response-assessable patients in Supplementary Figure S1, available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esmogo.2026.100334.

sec.p: Median PFS (95% CI) was 1.5 (1.4-2.6) months per investigator assessment and 1.7 (1.4-2.6) months per BICR, and median (95% CI) OS was 8.2 (2.2-13.9) months (Figure 1). 24-month rates for PFS per investigator assessment, PFS per BICR, and OS were 5%, 5%, and 17%, respectively (Figure 1).

sec.p: In post hoc exploratory analyses including 17 patients with available TMB data (median TMB, 4.98 mutations/Mb), patients with higher TMB tended to have controlled disease (a PR or stable disease), whereas patients with lower TMB tended to have progressive disease or an undeterminable response (Supplementary Figure S2, available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esmogo.2026.100334). There was also a trend toward numerically longer PFS and OS in patients with TMB at or above versus below the median TMB (Supplementary Figure S2, available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esmogo.2026.100334).

sec.title: Exposure and safety
sec.p: The median (range) number of doses received was 3 (1-75) for nivolumab, 1 (1-25) for ipilimumab, and 46 (1-458) for cobimetinib, and a relative dose intensity of ≥90% was received by 70% of treated patients for both nivolumab and ipilimumab, but only 37% of treated patients for cobimetinib (Supplementary Table S2, available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esmogo.2026.100334). Median (range) duration of treatment with nivolumab plus ipilimumab plus cobimetinib was 1.8 (0.3-37.2) months.

Safety outcomes are summarized in Table 3. Any-grade, any-cause AEs were reported in all 30 treated patients, with grade 3-4 events in 19 (63%), and grade 5 events in 6 (20%). Any-grade TRAEs were reported in 25 patients (83%), with grade 3-4 events in 9 (30%), and no grade 5 events. The most common any-grade TRAEs were blood creatinine phosphokinase increased (43%) and diarrhea (30%). Three patients (10%) discontinued treatment due to TRAEs, which included serous retinopathy, myelitis, pneumonitis, and rash. Serious TRAEs occurred in three patients (10%), and included myelitis, pneumonitis, and intestinal perforation.

sec.p: Any-grade endocrine TRAEs with potential immunologic etiology were reported in 4 patients (13%); of the patients experiencing non-endocrine TRAEs with potential immunologic etiology, 18 (60%) had skin-related events, 10 (33%) had hepatic events, 9 (30%) had gastrointestinal events, and 2 (7%) had pulmonary events (Supplementary Table S3, available at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.esmogo.2026.100334).

Overall, 28 patients died during the study; causes were disease progression (n = 22), infectious pneumonia and sepsis (1), septic shock (1), pneumatosis intestinalis (1), hepatic failure (1), and unknown reasons (2). No deaths were related to study drug toxicity.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this cohort of CheckMate 142, the combination of nivolumab, ipilimumab, and cobimetinib showed limited antitumor activity among patients with previously treated MSS/pMMR metastatic CRC, with an investigator-assessed ORR of 3%, DCR of 30%, median PFS of 1.5 months, and median OS of 8.2 months. Of the 30 treated patients, only 1 achieved an investigator-assessed objective response (a PR), although the TTR was relatively short (3 months) and the response was durable (DOR of 32.6 months). The nivolumab plus ipilimumab and cobimetinib regimen was generally well tolerated with no unexpected TRAEs observed. The limited antitumor activity observed with nivolumab plus ipilimumab and cobimetinib in this study aligns with results from the phase III IMblaze370 trial, which showed that a combination of atezolizumab (a programmed death ligand 1 ICI) and cobimetinib did not improve OS compared with regorafenib (a standard-of-care multi-kinase inhibitor) among patients with previously treated, predominantly MSS, metastatic CRC.17

In post hoc exploratory analyses in this MSS/pMMR cohort, DCRs were improved in patients with better ECOG PS, no liver metastases, and wild-type KRAS/BRAF. However, these observations should be interpreted cautiously since they were based on small subgroup sizes and most of these characteristics (e.g. better ECOG PS, absence of liver metastases, and wild-type BRAF) are known positive prognostic factors for patients with metastatic CRC, and are unlikely to be specifically predictive of response to nivolumab plus ipilimumab and cobimetinib.2,3,18 In additional post hoc exploratory analyses, efficacy benefits were also observed among patients with higher TMB. Although these analyses were again based on small sample sizes, this observation aligns with ancillary results from the AtezoTRIBE study showing that benefits of the addition of atezolizumab to a standard chemotherapy plus vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) inhibitor combination regimen were greater in patients with pMMR metastatic CRC and high versus low TMB.19

Unless eligible for specific biomarker-driven therapy, most patients with previously treated MSS/pMMR metastatic CRC will receive second-line treatment with chemotherapy alone or combined with a targeted agent, most commonly an inhibitor of VEGF or epidermal growth factor receptor.2,3 Results from the present study, along with those from prior studies demonstrating limited antitumor activity with ICI monotherapy or combinations of ICIs,10, 11, 12 indicate that purely ICI-based regimens are unlikely to find a role in the treatment of unselected populations with MSS/pMMR metastatic CRC. Nevertheless, recent results have shown encouraging efficacy and safety of first-line combinations of an ICI, chemotherapy, and a VEGF inhibitor in patients with MSS/pMMR metastatic CRC with a high immune infiltrate.19,20 This suggests a potential role for the addition of ICIs to current standard therapeutic regimens for treatment of select populations with MSS/pMMR metastatic CRC.

In conclusion, the data show that treatment with nivolumab plus ipilimumab and cobimetinib provided limited clinical benefit for patients with previously treated MSS/pMMR metastatic CRC and, based on these results, further study of this regimen is not warranted.
